_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss (Owen obliged to move vs Nadia moving when she likes; Owen's chores vs Bridget's shared cooking; Lucas not missing his things vs Bridget missing her kitchen; Nadia's mother's doubts vs Owen's own expectation). Used by the Part 7 practice page and by Full test 6.
title: Home, but not as you know it
subtitle: Four people describe life in an unusual home.

sections.A: Owen, 34, canal boat. I bought my narrowboat six years ago, mainly because it cost less than a deposit on a flat, and I assumed I'd live on it for a year at most. Without a permanent mooring, the rules say I have to move to a new spot at least every fourteen days, so I've got used to waking up to a different view every fortnight. What I hadn't got used to, at first, was how long ordinary things take. Filling the water tank, emptying the toilet, carrying coal along the towpath in January: none of it is difficult, but a whole quiet Sunday can disappear. The boating community makes up for it. People you met in spring turn up again in autumn a hundred miles away, and there's always someone who'll lend you a tool. Nobody stays put, yet I've never felt so much part of something.
sections.B: Nadia, 27, converted bus. The bus used to take children to a school in the next county, and when I bought it at auction it still smelled of crisps. I'd never so much as put up a shelf, but I spent eighteen months turning it into a home, learning almost everything from online videos and, when those failed, from a very patient man at the hardware shop. My mum was convinced I'd give up within a month; she now tells everyone it was her idea. I work online as a translator, so I can park wherever there's a signal, and I move on whenever I feel like a change. The only real downside is suspicion. More than once I've been woken at midnight by someone knocking to ask whether I'm allowed to be there. I always am, and I keep the paperwork by the bed.
sections.C: Lucas, 23, tiny city flat. My flat is eighteen square metres, which is roughly the size of my parents' living room. The bed folds up into the wall, the table folds down from it, and I can cook dinner while sitting on the sofa, which is either very convenient or slightly depressing, depending on my mood. Moving in meant getting rid of almost everything I owned; I sold three boxes of books and a guitar I'd never learned to play, and I honestly haven't missed any of it. The trick is not to think of the flat as my whole home. The park across the road is my garden, the library is my study, and the café downstairs is where I see friends, because only two people fit in here at once. For a lot less rent than a normal flat, I live in the middle of everything.
sections.D: Bridget, 58, shared farmhouse. Three families, eleven people and one enormous kitchen: that's our home. We'd been friends for years, and when the farmhouse came up for sale none of us could afford it alone, so we sold our own houses and bought it together. Each family has its own wing, but we cook and eat together four nights a week, taking turns, which means I make dinner for eleven once a fortnight and the rest of the time it simply appears. The only thing I miss is having a kitchen to myself. Of course there are disagreements, mostly about washing-up, but every Sunday evening we sit down and go through anything that's bothering anyone before it has time to grow. When my granddaughter was born last year, there were suddenly six people offering to babysit, which my daughter says got her through those first months.

questions.question: Which person created their home despite having almost no practical experience?
questions.why: 'I'd never so much as put up a shelf, but I spent eighteen months turning it into a home.' Bridget and her friends bought a farmhouse; nothing says they did any building.

questions.question: Which person describes a regular meeting that stops small problems becoming serious?
questions.why: 'Every Sunday evening we sit down and go through anything that's bothering anyone before it has time to grow.'

questions.question: Which person thought at first that their way of living would only be temporary?
questions.why: 'I assumed I'd live on it for a year at most.' Nadia's mother expected her to give up, but that was her mother's view, not Nadia's.

questions.question: Which person uses places nearby to make up for a lack of space indoors?
questions.why: 'The park across the road is my garden, the library is my study, and the café downstairs is where I see friends, because only two people fit in here.'

questions.question: Which person has work that allows them to change location whenever they choose?
questions.why: As a translator working online she can 'move on whenever I feel like a change'. Owen also moves often, but the rules force him to, every fourteen days.

questions.question: Which person finds that basic household tasks use up a lot of their free time?
questions.why: Filling the water tank and carrying coal mean 'a whole quiet Sunday can disappear'. Bridget's arrangement does the opposite: most nights dinner 'simply appears'.

questions.question: Which person mentions how their home helped a family member through a demanding period?
questions.why: Six people offered to babysit, 'which my daughter says got her through those first months' with the new baby.

questions.question: Which person has not regretted giving up most of their possessions?
questions.why: He sold books and a guitar and 'honestly haven't missed any of it'. Bridget sold her house and does miss something: 'having a kitchen to myself'.

questions.question: Which person feels they belong among people who rarely stay in one place for long?
questions.why: Boaters turn up 'a hundred miles away'; 'Nobody stays put, yet I've never felt so much part of something.' Bridget's group is close too, but it lives permanently in one house.

questions.question: Which person has had to show strangers that they have permission to be where they are?
questions.why: People knock 'to ask whether I'm allowed to be there', so she keeps 'the paperwork by the bed'. Owen follows the mooring rules, but nobody is said to question him.
